queries: [Page 78] II. FACILITY DESCRIPTION The Discharger provides sewerage service for the University of California, Davis and serves a campus population of approximately 48,000. The design daily average flow capacity of the Facility is 3.6 MGD. A. Description of Wastewater and Biosolids Treatment and Controls The treatment system at the Facility consists of manual and mechanical bar screens; an oxidation ditch activated sludge process with nitrification and denitrification, secondary clarifiers, gravity sand filter, disk cloth filter, and ultraviolet light (UV) disinfection system. Biosolids treatment consists of solids stabilization basins and sludge drying beds. Each summer, stabilized sludge is pumped into the drying beds for dewatering. Dewatered biosolids are transported and disposed at the Yolo County Central Landfill, a Class III non-hazardous municipal landfill as daily cover. Dried biosolids are stored onsite at the location(s) identified in Attachment C and are hauled to a landfill for disposal. Transportation and disposal/reuse of the biosolids is regulated by U.S. EPA under 40 C.F.R. part 503. B. Discharge Points and Receiving Waters 1. The Facility is located in Section 21, T8N, R2E, MDB&M, as shown in Attachment B, a part of this Order. 2. Treated municipal wastewater is discharged at Discharge Point No. 001 to the South Fork of Putah Creek, a water of the United States

chunks.text: The secondary clarifier is a 10-layer non-reactive system labelled from the bottom to the top. It has a total height of 4 m, and occupies a surface area of 1500 m 2 and a volume of 6000 m 3 . The tank is fed from the 6th, treated water is harvested from the 10th, and the settled sludge flows out from the first layer. A fraction of the sludge flows out of the system in the form of waste at a flow rate of 385 m 3 /d, corresponding to a biomass age of 9 days, while the other fraction is recycled externally to the first tank at a rate of 18,446 m 3 /d. The biological processes occurring in both biological reactors are simulated using the IWA Activated Sludge Model No. 1 (ASM1) proposed by [47] . This model uses thirteen state variables to track the fate of biodegradable, non-biodegradable, soluble, insoluble, nitrogen, and carbon materials. These state variables are linked to eight degradation bioprocesses occurring in biological reactors.

chunks.text: A pilot-scale system, consisting of a grit tank and microscreen for primary treatment followed by a SAF-MBR 2.0 for secondary treatment, was installed at the Codiga Resource Recovery Center (Stanford, CA), as illustrated in. The pilot-scale system treated municipal wastewater pumped from the Serra Street sewer on the Stanford campus for more than three years. Sewage was de-gritted in a grit tank then subject to primary treatment by screening through a 0.3 mm pore size microscreen (MS-28, Hydro International). The pilot-scale SAF-MBR 2.0 consisted of: (1) two AFBRs operated in parallel, hereafter referred to as AFBR 1 and AFBR 2, containing fluidized GAC biocarrier, and (2) a gas-sparged membrane tank equipped with ultrafiltration membranes. Recirculation of bulk fluid (twice the influent flow rate) between the three reactors enabled complete mixing and control of solids accumulation within the gas-sparged membrane tank.

chunks.text: A pilot-scale plexiglas Carrousel oxidation ditch was constructed, in which three semicircular channels were connected to four 1.15-m long straight channels. The ditch was 0.35-m wide and 0.5-m deep with a total working volume of 1.4 m 3 . Air was introduced from four 1-m long microporous aerator pipes located at the base of the second and third channels. The sketch of the reactor can be found in the supplementary information (SI). Experimental activated sludge was seeded from a steady-running SBR process in a municipal WWTP. The COD and NH 4 + -N concentration of synthetic wastewater were controlled at 250 mg L −1 and 50 mg L −1 , and pH was approximately 7.8 without adjustment. The liquor temperature was maintained at 22 ± 2 °C with a heating rod. Before getting into the inlet of the first channel, the influent and returned sludge were firstly pumped into a 50-L bioselector with continuous blending to avoid sludge bulking problem. The variations of HRT and SRT were achieved by altering the daily influent and sludge discharge rate.

chunks.citation: Ma, Y et al. (2009). Achieving nitrogen removal via nitrite in a pilot-scale continuous pre-denitrification plant. nan.
chunks.text:
The traditional biological nitrogen removal processes utilized in wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) involve the oxidation of ammonium (NH 4 þ ) to nitrate (NO 3 À ) (nitrification) followed by nitrate reduction with an organic carbon source to nitrogen gas (N 2 ) (denitrification). Both nitrification and denitrification possess nitrite (NO 2 À ) as an intermediate. Hence, if

nitrification is stopped at nitrite, denitritation from nitrite to nitrogen gas can be achieved (Verstraete et al., 1977) . Nitrogen removal via nitrite yields 25% reduction in oxygen demand for nitrification and 40% reduction in chemical oxygen demand (COD) requirement for denitrification (Pollice et al., 2002; Turk and Mavinic, 1987) . The reduction in COD requirement would be particularly advantageous for WWTPs treating wastewater with a low COD to nitrogen ratio.

chunks.text: Advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) represent a diverse array of water treatment technologies that have generated significant research attention and utilization in a range of water and wastewater treatment applications over the years [1] . Many of the potential and demonstrated applications of AOPs are related to the treatment of industrial wastewater effluents, including those generated from hospitals, slaughterhouses, distilleries, textile mills, and chemical processing plants [2] . Depending on the source, industrial effluents can contain a mixture of complex pollutants, including recalcitrant and toxic organic compounds such as aromatics, pesticides, pharmaceuticals, personal care products, and endocrine-disrupting chemicals. AOPs have been identified as an effective means to treat these complex effluents due to their ability to produce powerful oxidizing agents such as hydroxyl radicals ( • OH) insitu [3] . The strength and non-selectivity of • OH as an oxidizing agent enables the complete mineralization of a wide range of organic compounds at first order rates in the magnitude of 10 6 to 10 9 M − 1 s − 1 [4] .

chunks.text: The drying facility is located in a large Polish wastewater treatment plant and is composed of 4 lines. The scheme of one drying line is presented in Fig. 1 . Dewatered sludge is collected in a silo from where it is dosed to drum dryers. The temperature in the drum dryers is maintained at ca. 240-260 • C using hot oil. Sludge is uniformly distributed in the drum with paddles. The sludge retention time in the drier is 1-2 min, and the sludge layer in the drum is 1-2 cm thick. Water from the sludge is evaporated and flows as condensate with process air through a purification system composed of a Venturi orifice and two scrubbers, where it is then rinsed with the process water (secondary effluent from the wastewater treatment plant). During rinsing, particulate matter, as well as soluble gases such as ammonia are captured by the process water, and Fig. 1 . Scheme of the drying line. chunks.text: A process flow diagram (Fig. 1a ) shows the key elements of the activated sludge system. Some systems have slightly different configurations (e.g., inclusion of primary treatment); however, the configurations shown were typical of most sites in the study. Use of biosolid dewatering varied across sites with some utilizing belt filter presses, some others utilizing drying beds, and several not utilizing any form at all. The main difference among technologies is the secondary treatment, where OD and EA use different reactor configurations in conjunction with a clarifier for treatment and SBRs use multiple basins for aeration and settling. It should be noted that none of the sites used primary clarifier. In most cases, decanted water from biosolids was also recycled back to the front of facility. Auxiliary infrastructure includes buildings for housing equipment, vehicles, lab, and related components.

chunks.text: In the activated sludge process the majority of biological solids removed in the secondary sedimentation tank are recycled (returned sludge). The feedback of most of the cell yields from the sedimentation tank encourages rapid adsorption of the pollutants in the incoming settled sewage and also serves to stabilize the operation over a wide range of dilution rates and substrate concentrations imposed by fluctuations in the flow and strength of the wastewater. Secondary treatment processes can remove up to 95 per cent of the BOD and suspended solids entering the process, as well as significant amounts of heavy metals and certain organic compounds which could otherwise cause the deterioration of chemical and ecological quality of receiving waters [10, 53] . Conventional wastewater treatment usually ends with secondary treatment which cannot efficiently remove all the different compounds found in sewage and therefore treated effluents are one of the main sources of persistent micropollutants in the environment [1, 62] . For water reuse, tertiary treatment is needed to provide additional removal of contaminants such as microbial pathogens, particulates, or nutrients, and advanced treatment processes are employed when wastewater is to be reclaimed for reuse, depending on the type of use and quality requirements [49] .

chunks.text: Based on a survey on pre-treatment measures for 17 full-scale AeMBRs, the following information deserves special attention (Itokawa et al., 2008) : 1) grit chamber, coarse and fine screenings are mostly essential for MBR operation to removal grits, large suspended particles and long fibers, with fine screening (3 mm for FS membrane and 0.5-1 mm for HF membrane) installed universally; and 2) using the "by pass sieving" method, which recycles part of the suspended sludge through a sieve, achieves the further removal of unfavorable substances accumulated in the bioreactor. These means can be extended to AnMBRs minimizing the presence of undesirable substances into the bioreactor while with adequate consideration of keeping strict anaerobic environment. A recent novel concept, referred to as wastewater pre-concentration (Ansari et al., 2016) , is still under investigation, but has shown great potential to enhance bioresource recovery and energy generation efficiency (Guven et al., 2019) , accompanied by a low volumetric flow rate and process footprint (Alvarado et al., 2020) .

chunks.text: Continuing urbanization has placed a formidable burden on wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) (Du et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2019) . The development of innovative solutions that can intensify wastewater treatment processes becomes imperative. Anaerobic ammonium oxidation (anammox) technology offers the potential to enhance wastewater treatment capacity owing to its remarkably reduced sludge production in a fully autotrophic nitrogen removal process (Jetten et al., 1997; Kuenen, 2008) . In addition, anammox processes have also demonstrated impressive high-rate capabilities, achieving nitrogen removal rates of up to 7.5 kg N/(m 3 d) in mainstream wastewater (Cheng et al., 2020; Tang et al., 2011; Yokota et al., 2018; Hou et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023a) .
